prompt: A nightly export is switched from a 40 GB CSV to Parquet. The same `SELECT customer_id, amount FROM export WHERE amount > 500` drops from 90 seconds to 4, on the same hardware. Walk through what about the file layout produced that drop.
criteria: Names columnar storage as why only the two requested columns are read
Mentions compression reducing the bytes pulled off disk
States that CSV forces a read of every row and every column
Says typed columns remove per-value string parsing at read time

prompt: Name a situation where handing someone a CSV is the better call than Parquet, and say what you are giving up by doing it.
criteria: Names a consumer that cannot read Parquet, such as a spreadsheet or a shell tool
States that a person can open CSV and read it with no library
Names what is lost: declared types, compression, column pruning
Mentions the file growing much larger as the price paid

prompt: A Parquet file keeps the minimum and maximum value of each column for every row group. A query filters `WHERE order_date = '2026-03-01'`. What does the reader do with those statistics?
options: Skips whole row groups whose min/max range cannot contain that date
Rewrites the filter as a range scan across the entire file
Sorts the rows by order_date before applying the filter
Uses them to pick a faster decompression algorithm

prompt: Which of these statements are true of a Parquet file but not of a CSV file holding the same rows?
options: Every column carries a declared data type stored in the file itself
The values of a single column sit contiguously rather than scattered across rows
The reader can skip a block of rows without decoding it, using stored min/max values
A text editor shows you the contents with no extra tooling
Adding one record means appending a single line to the end of the file

prompt: A product manager notices that one dashboard shows signups as of four hours ago while another shows them as of a minute ago, and both are described as reading the same table. Explain the difference without assuming they know SQL.
criteria: States that one reads saved results while the other runs the query fresh
Names the refresh schedule as the source of the four-hour gap
Gives the reason the saved copy exists, such as speed or query cost
Ends on a decision for them to make, such as how fresh the number needs to be

prompt: A team swaps a heavily used view for a materialized view refreshed nightly at 02:00, and the morning numbers match exactly. What breaks first, and who is the first person to notice?
criteria: Names staleness: anything changing between refreshes stays invisible until the next one
Identifies a consumer who needs intraday numbers as the first to complain
Mentions a refresh that fails silently while yesterday's rows keep serving
Says an upstream schema change can break the refresh without breaking the reads

prompt: True or false: wrapping an expensive query in a view makes that query cheaper for everyone who then selects from the view.
criteria: States that a view stores the query text and no result rows
Says the underlying query executes again on every reference to the view
Names materialization as the thing that would actually save the repeated work
Notes the view still earns its keep by keeping the logic in one place

prompt: Fill in the blanks: a ______ holds only the query definition and re-executes it on every read, while a ______ holds the query's output and shows new rows only once it has been refreshed.

A team keeps 8 TB in warehouse storage and runs roughly 300 analyst queries a day on a warehouse that auto-suspends after one minute of idle time. Storage bills at about $23 per TB-month and compute at about $3 per credit-hour. Rough out where the monthly bill lands and name the lever worth pulling.
criteria: Puts storage near $180 to $200 a month at that rate
States an assumption about how many hours a day the warehouse is active
Gives compute as a range rather than one precise figure
Names the lever as idle time or bytes scanned, not deleting stored data

prompt: A manager reads the warehouse invoice, decides it is too high, and asks the team to start deleting raw history to bring it down. Push back.
criteria: States that storage and compute are billed as two separate lines
Names query compute as the larger share of that invoice
Names what deleting raw history costs: no backfill, no reprocessing after a bug
Offers a concrete alternative such as a shorter auto-suspend or pruning scans

prompt: Two teams query the same 5 TB table. One runs a single query an hour, the other runs a hundred. On a warehouse that separates storage from compute, how do their bills differ?
options: Storage is billed once for the table regardless of reads, so the busier team's extra cost is all compute time
The busier team pays more for storage, because each read re-charges the bytes it touched
Both bills come out the same, since the table is one size and both read all of it
The busier team's queries are free, because the storage charge already covers reading the data

prompt: Match each thing a team does in the warehouse to the bill it actually lands on.
left: Keeping seven years of raw event files that nobody has queried since
An analyst kicking off a full-table scan over 2 TB at noon
A warehouse left running with no query submitted for ten minutes
Cloning a 2 TB table to give a test environment its own copy
right: Compute billed for the seconds the query spends executing
Almost nothing extra, because only blocks that change are stored twice
Storage, which grows slowly and stays cheap per terabyte
Compute billed for idle seconds until auto-suspend takes effect

prompt: A teammate adds `*:focus { outline: none; }` to the stylesheet because the blue ring looked out of place on the cards, and ships it. Critique that change.
criteria: Names the keyboard user who can no longer tell where they are on the page
States that focus still moves, only the indicator of it is gone
Proposes restyling the ring, such as with :focus-visible, instead of deleting it
Notes that a mouse user never sees the problem, which is why it ships unnoticed

prompt: Someone hands you a drill app and takes the mouse away. Describe how you would get through one card using only the keyboard, and what each step tells you about the markup underneath.
criteria: Names Tab as the way focus moves between interactive elements
States that Enter or Space activates a real button element
Says an element that never receives focus is not a button in the markup
Mentions tab order following document order unless tabindex overrides it

prompt: One line below leaves a control that a person without a mouse can never reach or fire. Which line?
why: A `div` is not in the tab order and does not fire its click handler on Enter or Space, so Submit can never be reached or activated from the keyboard — and the `.btn:focus` rule never matches anything, because the element never takes focus. The Skip control gets the tab stop, the key handling and the announced role for free by being a `<button>`.

prompt: Fill in the blanks: a label is tied to its field either by wrapping the field or by pointing the label's ______ attribute at the field's ______ value, which is what makes clicking the label text move focus into the field.
JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, yet a page stays responsive while three network requests are in flight. Explain how both of those are true at the same time.
criteria: States that the network wait is handed to the runtime, not run on the JS thread
Says callbacks are queued and run only when the call stack empties
Names a long synchronous loop as the thing that does freeze the page
Draws the line between waiting on I/O and doing CPU work

prompt: A loader walks 5,000 ids, calls an async `fetchRow(id)` for each without awaiting it, pushes each return value into an array, and hands that array back. What breaks first?
criteria: States the array holds pending Promises rather than rows
Names 5,000 requests all in flight at once as the load problem
Mentions rate limiting, connection limits or memory as the first visible failure
Names batching with Promise.all, or awaiting in the loop, as the fix

prompt:
A helper is defined and called without `await`:

`async function load() {`
`  return 42;`
`}`
`const value = load();`
`console.log(typeof value, value instanceof Promise);`

What gets logged?
accept: object true — it is a Promise, not 42
explain: An async function always returns a Promise, even when its body returns a plain number. Without `await`, `value` is that Promise wrapper: `typeof` reports `object` and the `instanceof` check is `true`. The 42 is only reachable through `await load()` or `load().then(...)`.

prompt:
A script runs these four lines top to bottom:

`console.log('one');`
`setTimeout(() => console.log('two'), 0);`
`Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('three'));`
`console.log('four');`

Put the four logs in the order their output actually appears.
Give a layout where reaching for CSS grid is the wrong call, and say what flexbox does better there.
criteria: Names a one-dimensional case such as a toolbar or a row of pips
States that flexbox sizes items from their content rather than from declared tracks
Mentions that grid makes you commit to tracks the content may not fit
Names wrapping or space distribution along one axis as the flex strength

prompt: A teammate builds a card by giving it `position: relative` and placing its title, body and footer with `position: absolute` at fixed pixel offsets, on the grounds that it lines up pixel for pixel with the mock. Critique that.
criteria: States that absolutely positioned children are taken out of normal flow
Names longer or translated text as what then overflows or overlaps
Mentions that the card can no longer size itself to its own content
Names a flex column or grid rows as the layout that grows with the text

prompt: Which of these are reasons to reach for CSS grid rather than flexbox?
options: Items have to line up across rows and down columns at the same time
You want to name regions of a page and drop children into them by name
A row of items should size to its content and wrap onto a second line
Two items need to sit at opposite ends of one bar with the gap in between
You want to declare the track sizes up front and have children land in them

prompt: A row of fixed-size progress pips looks right on a wide screen, but the pips squash into slivers as the window narrows. One line causes it — which?
why: `flex-shrink: 1` is the default, and it lets every pip give up width once the line runs short, so the declared `12px` is only a starting size rather than a floor. `flex-shrink: 0` pins each pip at 12px and forces the row to wrap or scroll instead of shrinking its children.
